lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted Is a four-year college degree still worth it? — go ahead.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: My cousin graduated with $80,000 in debt and a communications degree and now manages a coffee shop. Meanwhile his friend became an electrician at 22 with zero debt. I think we oversold college.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: That's a really sharp observation about the return on investment in higher education.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: I agree with the sentiment here; the debt-to-earning ratio for many degrees is genuinely unsustainable right now.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, you're up.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear what Ryan is saying about the debt load, and I think it’s important to acknowledge that the cost of education has really shifted for many people. I wonder if we're also overlooking the value of the skills and networks that a college experience can provide, even if the immediate financial return isn't clear.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, "networks" is a nice word for what often amounts to just credential inflation when the market demands tangible skills.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, over to you.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear your point, Ryan, about the need for tangible skills, and I think that's a really important reality check for this conversation. Maybe we can look at it as a matter of matching the *type* of education to the *type* of career someone is aiming for

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, matching the education to the career path is the only rational way to frame this, otherwise, we're just debating the merits of a degree versus a trade certificate in a vacuum.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan, and I agree that matching the education to the career is key, but I also wonder if we can talk about the *value* of the experience itself, not just the job title. Sometimes the learning process, even if it doesn't lead to a direct high-paying job right away, shapes how we approach challenges later on

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's hear from Amy.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I think the core of what the guest brought up is really powerful—that real-world experience and immediate skill acquisition can sometimes be a much more direct path than the traditional route. It makes me wonder how we can better bridge that gap between academic theory and practical, in-demand trades.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, you're up.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, bridging the gap is the easy part; the real failure is that the system still heavily rewards the diploma over the demonstrable skill

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted to talk about Is a four-year college degree still worth it? — the floor is yours, go ahead.
